fetched_contents.title: NDBC - Does NDBC adjust C-MAN and buoy wind speed observations to a standard height?
fetched_contents.text: NDBC Does NDBC adjust C-MAN and buoy wind speed observations to a standard height? Yes, but we only list the standardized wind speeds where those who need them look for them. Anemometer heights on NDBC buoys vary according to buoy type. Anemometers on 3-meter discus and 6-meter NOMAD buoys are located approximately 5 meters above the waterline. Anemometers on 10 and 12-meter buoys are located 10 meters above the waterline. Anemometer heights at CMAN stations vary widely, depending on site structure and elevation above sea level. NDBC adjusts wind speeds to conform to the universally accepted reference standard of 10 meters. NDBC also adjusts wind speeds to 20 meters, a height closer to that typical of ship anemometers. This is done to provide marine forecasters and data modelers a means to directly compare buoy observations with ship observations. These height standardized wind speeds may be found in the last two columns of the files in the derived2 data directory. Only unadjusted wind speeds as actually measured by station anemometers are posted in the data sections of the station pages on the NDBC website, retained in the historical data pages, and archived at the national archive centers. The method used by NDBC to adjust wind speeds to a standard reference level is described by W. T. Liu et al. (1979). The method iteratively solves equations involving the air-sea exchanges of momentum, heat, and water vapor to arrive at the wind speed profile in the lower atmospheric boundary layer. Air and water temperature, wind speed at the height of observation, and relative humidity are required inputs to the algorithm. Since relative humidity is usually not measured, it is assumed to be 85 percent. A simpler method is described by S. A. Hsu et al. (1994). Although never used operationally by NDBC, the method was tested and found to compare favorably with the more elaborate method under near-neutral stability. This is the condition most frequently encountered at sea and occurs when air and water temperatures are not too far apart. The method, referred to as the Power Law Method, is offered here for those who may want to explore the nature of the marine wind speed profile without having to deal with the complexity of the above method. The relationship is: u2 = u1 (z2/z1)P where u2 is the wind speed at the desired reference height, z2, and u1 is the wind speed measured at height z1. A value for the exponent, P, equal to 0.11 was empirically determined to be applicable most of the time over the ocean. References: Hsu, S. A., Eric A. Meindl, and David B. Gilhousen, 1994: Determining the Power-Law Wind-Profile Exponent under Near-Neutral Stability Conditions at Sea, Applied Meteorology, Vol. 33, No. 6, June 1994. Liu, W. T., K. B. Katsaros, and J. A. Businger, 1979: Bulk Parameterizations of Air-Sea Exchanges of Heat and Water Vapor Including Molecular Constraints at the Interface, Journal of Atmospheric Science, Vol. 36, 1722-1735. ----------------------------------------

fetched_contents.text: Wind profile power law Relationship of wind speeds at varying heights The wind profile power law is a relationship between the wind speeds at one height, and those at another. Definition The wind profile power law relationship is u u r = ( z z r ) α {\displaystyle {\frac {u}{u_{r}}}={\bigg (}{\frac {z}{z_{r}}}{\bigg )}^{\alpha }} where u {\displaystyle u} is the wind speed (in metres per second) at height z {\displaystyle z} (in metres), and u r {\displaystyle u_{r}} is the known wind speed at a reference height z r {\displaystyle z_{r}} . The exponent ( α {\displaystyle \alpha } ) is an empirically derived coefficient that varies dependent upon the stability of the atmosphere. For neutral stability conditions, α {\displaystyle \alpha } is approximately 1/7, or 0.143. In order to estimate the wind speed at a certain height z, the relationship would be rearranged to u = u r ( z z r ) α {\displaystyle u=u_{r}{\bigg (}{\frac {z}{z_{r}}}{\bigg )}^{\alpha }} The value of 1/7 for α is commonly assumed to be constant in wind resource assessments, because the differences between the two levels are not usually so great as to introduce substantial errors into the estimates (usually < 50 m). However, when a constant exponent is used, it does not account for the roughness of the surface, the displacement of calm winds from the surface due to the presence of obstacles (i.e., zero-plane displacement), or the stability of the atmosphere.[1][2] In places where trees or structures impede the near-surface wind, the use of a constant 1/7 exponent may yield quite erroneous estimates, and the log wind profile is preferred. Even under neutral stability conditions, an exponent of 0.11 is more appropriate over open water (e.g., for offshore wind farms), than 0.143,[3] which is more applicable over open land surfaces. Limits The wind profile of the atmospheric boundary layer (surface to around 2000 metres) is generally logarithmic in nature and is best approximated using the log wind profile equation that accounts for surface roughness and atmospheric stability. The relationships between surface power and wind are often used as an alternative to logarithmic wind features when surface roughness or stability information is not available. Applications The power law is often used in wind power assessments[4][5] where wind speeds at the height of a turbine ( ≥ {\displaystyle \geq } 50 metres) must be estimated from near surface wind observations (~10 metres), or where wind speed data at various heights must be adjusted to a standard height[6] prior to use. ## Technical basis for height adjustment to 10 meters

The adjustment from one height to another is grounded in the vertical structure of the atmospheric boundary layer. The most common analytical frameworks are the **logarithmic wind profile** and the **power-law wind profile**, with the former generally regarded as the more physically accurate approximation for the surface layer and the latter serving as a simpler empirical substitute where roughness or stability information is limited [N2-F2] [N2-R3].

### Which formulas or profiles are used to relate wind speed at one height to another?

The wind profile power law provides the simplest direct formula for relating wind speeds at two heights:
$$
u_2 = u_1 \left( \frac{z_2}{z_1} \right)^\alpha
$$
where $ u_1 $ is the measured wind speed at height $ z_1 $, $ u_2 $ is the wind speed at height $ z_2 $, and $ \alpha $ is the power-law exponent [N2-F2]. This relationship is often rearranged to estimate a known reference wind speed from an observed wind speed at a different height [N2-F2].

The logarithmic wind profile is the more physically justified formulation for the surface layer and is best approximated by:
$$
\frac{u}{u_*} = \frac{1}{\kappa} \ln \left( \frac{z}{z_0} \right)
$$
where $ u_* $ is the friction velocity, $ \kappa $ is the von Kármán constant, and $ z_0 $ is the roughness length [N2-R1] [N2-R3]. In the context of adjustment, this means that wind speed at a target height is inferred from the logarithmic relationship between height, friction velocity, and roughness length, rather than from a simple power-law exponent alone [N2-R3].

A practical adjustment tool such as the Wind Data calculator explicitly uses a reference height $ h_1 $, a target height $ h_2 $, and the roughness length $ z_0 $ to estimate the wind speed at the target height from a known reference wind speed [N6-R2].

### How roughness length, stability, and height scaling affect the adjustment

The adjustment depends strongly on the **roughness length $ z_0 $** and the **atmospheric stability** because these determine the shape of the wind profile. The Wikipedia entry states that the power-law exponent varies with stability, and for neutral stability it is approximately 1/7 (0.143), whereas over open water the exponent used in offshore wind farms is more appropriately 0.11 [N2-F2]. This means that a naive power-law transfer can give incorrect results if the adjustment does not account for the local stability regime [N2-F2].

The **logarithmic profile** explicitly incorporates $ z_0 $, so roughness length is a central parameter in the adjustment process [N2-R3]. The profile also depends on stability through the gradient of the wind speed with height, which changes under stable, neutral, and unstable conditions [N2-R4] [N2-R1]. In other words, the same observed wind speed at one height can imply very different values at another height if the adjustment ignores or misestimates $ z_0 $ and the stability class [N2-F2] [N2-R3].

The **height scaling** itself matters because the exponent in the power law and the logarithmic profile both depend on the ratio of the two heights, not just the absolute heights. The power-law relationship is:
$$
u = u_r \left( \frac{z}{z_r} \right)^\alpha
$$
so the adjustment is sensitive to the relative heights being connected [N2-F2]. The logarithmic profile is similarly scale-dependent because the logarithmic term increases with height, making the adjustment non-linear and more sensitive to large height differences [N2-R3].

### Whether the adjustment depends on friction velocity or other boundary layer parameters

The adjustment **can** depend on friction velocity, but this is not always explicit in the simpler power-law formulas. The logarithmic wind profile formulation makes friction velocity an implicit part of the adjustment because it defines the reference wind speed relative to the surface shear stress [N2-R3]. However, the **power-law method** often omits explicit reference to friction velocity and instead uses an empirical exponent, which is why it is described as a “simpler” alternative when surface roughness or stability information is not available [N2-F2].

More advanced methods, such as the NDBC adjustment described in the search result, use a full boundary-layer algorithm that solves equations involving air-sea exchanges of momentum, heat, and water vapor, and requires inputs such as air and water temperature, wind speed at the observation height, and relative humidity (assumed at 85% if not measured) [N1-F1]. That method is more comprehensive than a simple power-law or logarithmic transfer because it incorporates multiple boundary-layer parameters rather than relying on a single height-dependent exponent [N1-F1].

In short, the adjustment can depend on **friction velocity and related boundary-layer parameters** when using the logarithmic profile or a coupled boundary-layer scheme, but the power-law method usually depends instead on an empirically derived exponent that varies with stability and surface conditions [N2-F2] [N1-F1].

## Practical measurement and instrumentation considerations

### What heights are commonly measured and why

Wind speeds are commonly measured at several standard heights because different applications and instruments operate at different altitudes. The NDBC source explicitly notes that wind speeds are adjusted to 10 meters, but also that some observations are made at 5 meters, 10 meters, 20 meters, and even 10/12-meter buoys above the waterline [N1-F1]. In other contexts, meteorological stations and wind farms may measure at 20 meters, 40 meters, 60 meters, and even higher heights, especially when the data are needed for turbine design, energy assessment, or validation against high-altitude measurements [N3-F3] [N5-F4].

The 10-meter reference height is standard because it is widely accepted and provides a consistent basis for comparing observations across different sites and instruments [N1-F1]. The 20-meter height is also common because it is closer to the typical height of ship anemometers and is useful for comparing buoy and ship observations [N1-F1]. Higher heights such as 60 meters, 100 meters, or 120 meters are used when the goal is turbine-height wind assessment, tall-tower monitoring, or validation of high-altitude instruments such as sodar and lidar [N3-F3] [N5-F4].

### How tower layout and instrument placement affect height-dependent data

Tower layout and instrument placement strongly affect the height-dependent data because the structure itself modifies the local wind field. The IEA recommended practice notes that tower-induced flow modifications can alter anemometer measurements and that tower-mounted anemometers should be placed carefully to minimize flow disturbance [N3-F3]. The recommended practice also emphasizes separation between the anemometer rotor and the tower top, and it warns against sheared flow and other tower effects [N3-F3].

In practical terms, this means that wind speeds measured at different heights on the same tower can differ not only because of the actual wind profile, but also because the tower itself creates turbulence, wake effects, and flow distortion. The same issue appears in tall-tower monitoring, where cup anemometers are installed at 20, 40, and 60 meters, and sonic anemometers are also placed at 20 and 60 meters [N3-F3]. This layout is meant to capture the vertical wind structure, but it also means that each measurement is subject to tower interference to some degree [N3-F3].

Instrument placement also matters because anemometers are not always mounted at the same height relative to the ground. The NDBC source explains that anemometer heights vary with buoy type and station structure, and that the 10-meter reference is adjusted upward from the actual measurement height [N1-F1]. This implies that the raw data must be corrected to the standard height to be comparable across different systems [N1-F1].

### Common measurement artifacts or biases at different heights

Several measurement artifacts or biases can arise at different heights. The tower-induced flow issue is the most direct: tower effects can create turbulence, shear, and wake effects that distort the wind field and make the measured profile different from the true atmospheric profile [N3-F3]. The recommended practice also warns against sheared flow and emphasizes that these effects should be minimized in field practice [N3-F3].

Another common bias is the use of a constant power-law exponent. The Wikipedia entry notes that a constant exponent such as 1/7 is often assumed for wind resource assessments because the height differences are usually small enough not to introduce large errors, but that this assumption can be inaccurate when surface roughness or stability varies significantly [N2-F2]. It also states that over open water the exponent should often be 0.11 rather than 0.143, showing how simple empirical methods can be biased by site-specific conditions [N2-F2].

A third bias is the assumption of neutral stability. The power-law method is described as a simpler alternative under near-neutral stability, but the NDBC source says that the more elaborate method is tested and found to compare favorably with the simpler method under near-neutral conditions [N1-F1]. This means that the adjustment can be biased when the actual atmospheric state is not neutral, especially in stable or unstable regimes [N1-F1].

In addition, the recommended practice notes that wind speed measurements at different heights are affected by vertical sensitivity, overspeeding, dynamic filtering, and other behavior in the real atmosphere [N3-F3]. These issues suggest that the raw data are not always directly comparable across heights and that adjustment is often necessary to obtain a consistent 10-meter reference.

Overall, the practical measurement picture is that wind speeds are measured at multiple heights for different purposes, but tower layout and instrument placement can create artifacts, and the simplest power-law transfer may be biased if site-specific conditions such as roughness, stability, and tower interference are not properly accounted for [N3-F3] [N2-F2] [N1-F1].

## Modeling and application implications

### How adjusted 10-meter wind speed is used in NWP and boundary layer models

Adjusted 10-meter wind speed is a critical input for numerical weather prediction (NWP) and boundary layer modeling because many forecast variables are diagnosed or parameterized relative to the lowest model level. The search result on adaptive tuning notes that near-surface forecast variables such as 10-m wind speed are strongly affected by uncertain model parameters and that parameterization of subgrid-scale processes is needed to account for their effects on larger-scale forecast variables [N4-R4]. This implies that the 10-meter wind speed is not just a standalone observation but a central diagnostic quantity in the model state.

In boundary layer modeling, the 10-meter reference height is also important because it is the height at which many surface-layer parameterizations are defined. The NDBC adjustment method itself is described as solving equations involving air-sea exchanges of momentum, heat, and water vapor, and it is used to derive the wind speed profile in the lower atmospheric boundary layer [N1-F1]. That suggests that the adjusted 10-meter wind speed supports both surface flux closure and the vertical structure of the boundary layer in NWP.

The NWP and wind speed forecasting search result further indicates that operational NWP models are being developed to improve wind energy forecasts using multiscale datasets, and that statistical calibration models can improve numeric wind speed prediction by accounting for local conditions [N4-R1] [N4-R3]. This shows that the adjusted 10-meter wind speed is used not only as a diagnostic input but also as a basis for model corrections and forecasting improvements [N4-R1] [N4-R3].

### Which model parameterizations depend on the adjustment

Several model parameterizations depend on the height adjustment because many boundary-layer and turbulence closures are formulated relative to the surface layer. The logarithmic wind profile is a classic example: it depends on roughness length $ z_0 $, friction velocity $ u_* $, and the von Kármán constant $ \kappa $, and it is used to relate wind speed at one height to another [N2-R3]. In practice, this means that parameterizations such as surface fluxes, mixing-length closures, and surface-layer similarity laws depend on the adjusted 10-meter wind speed as a reference state [N2-R4].

The power-law method is also relevant because it is used to estimate wind speed at different heights from a known reference wind speed, and it is noted in the wind-resource context as a common tool for adjusting wind speeds to a standard height prior to use [N2-F2]. The search result also states that the power law is often used in wind power assessments and in atmospheric pollution dispersion models [N2-F2]. This implies that model parameterizations related to wind resource assessment, dispersion modeling, and energy forecasting depend on the height adjustment [N2-F2].

Another relevant implication is that the NDBC adjustment method itself is a boundary-layer closure, not just an empirical correction. It uses a coupled momentum, heat, and water vapor algorithm to derive the wind profile, which means that boundary-layer parameterizations such as drag, entrainment, and shear stress depend on the adjusted 10-meter wind speed as part of the model state [N1-F1].

### How errors or uncertainties propagate through the adjustment process

Errors and uncertainties propagate through the adjustment process in several ways. First, the adjustment depends on the choice of profile and the stability class. The power-law exponent varies with stability, so an incorrect assumption about stability can lead to a biased transfer [N2-F2]. Similarly, the logarithmic profile depends on $ z_0 $, so an incorrect roughness length can produce a different adjusted wind speed at the target height [N2-R3].

Second, the adjustment depends on the quality of the observed wind speed at the source height. If the observed wind speed is inaccurate, the adjusted wind speed will inherit that inaccuracy. The recommended practice notes that wind speed measurements are affected by vertical sensitivity, overspeeding, and dynamic filtering, which can introduce measurement errors that propagate into the adjustment [N3-F3].

Third, the adjustment depends on the uncertainty in the model parameters used to derive the boundary-layer state. The adaptive-tuning search result states that near-surface forecast variables like 10-m wind speed are strongly affected by uncertain model parameters such as those used to parameterize subgrid-scale processes [N4-R4]. This means that uncertainty in the parameterization can propagate into the adjusted wind speed and downstream forecasts.

Fourth, the adjustment can introduce errors if the assumed exponent is constant when the actual exponent varies with height, stability, or surface roughness. The Wikipedia entry explicitly notes that using a constant 1/7 exponent may be inaccurate in places where trees or structures impede the near-surface wind, and that the log wind profile is preferred in such cases [N2-F2]. This shows that the adjustment can propagate uncertainty into the final wind speed estimate and into any applications that depend on it.

In summary, adjusted 10-meter wind speed is central to NWP and boundary layer modeling because it supports surface-layer closure, subgrid-scale parameterization, and forecast diagnostics. The adjustment process depends on the chosen profile, stability, roughness length, and measurement quality, and errors in any of these factors propagate through the model and into downstream applications [N1-F1] [N2-F2] [N3-F3] [N4-R4].
